Biological vs Non‑Organic Memory — A Conceptual Bridge

Could non‑organic forms also have a form of memory? This note describes a bridge between biological and non‑organic memory, mapping biological (neural/immune/epigenetic) and non‑organic (physical/material) memory under a single definition.

Bridge Definition

Across living and non‑living systems, memory can be defined as a lasting, experience‑dependent state change that modulates future response. Biological realizations include synaptic plasticity, trained immunity, and epigenetic marks; non‑organic realizations include hysteresis loops, resistive switching, shape memory transformations, and history‑dependent microstructures.

Non‑Organic Memory

  • Magnetic & Ferroelectric hysteresis: system response depends on prior fields; used for non‑volatile data storage.
  • Shape memory alloys: martensite↔austenite transitions “remember” a trained shape recovered by heating.
  • Memristive devices: resistance encodes past current; a hardware analog to synaptic plasticity.
  • Glasses, polymers, and soft matter: aging and cyclic training store multiple memories of preparation or load history.
  • Geological archives: rocks and ice strata store Earth’s magnetic and climatic histories.
  • Dissipative structures: non‑equilibrium patterns reflect and “record” boundary conditions and flows.

Shared operations: write (exposure), store (structure), read (stimulus). Different substrates, same logic.
